# Improve UI

## Intent

Make the War Room board stable and central to the page, keep its supporting context easy to reach, let users set useful panel widths on different screens, and let users prioritize backlog features by dragging them. Improve the time to a usable board and the speed at which changes appear.

### Success criteria

- On wide screens, the In flight / chat context is left of the board, the board occupies the center, and the existing utility sidebar remains on the right. Board width does not jump when board data refreshes or cards change.
- Users can resize the three top-level panels within sensible bounds. The choice survives a reload on the same browser; a reset restores usable defaults. The page uses available viewport width rather than the present 1400px cap.
- At narrower widths the panels reflow without horizontal page overflow or hidden controls. The board remains usable, including selection, actions, chat, and backlog ordering.
- Backlog feature cards can be dragged to reorder priority within their epic. The resulting order is durable, is shared by board readers, survives refresh/reload, and is shown consistently wherever that backlog is rendered. An invalid or stale reorder has a clear failure and does not silently replace newer order.
- The initial board is usable within 2 seconds in the agreed local benchmark; ordinary board actions and incoming state changes provide prompt visible feedback. A reproducible before/after performance review identifies and fixes the material bottlenecks rather than adding speculative caching.

## Macro-architecture

The War Room remains a server-rendered HTML shell with CSS and plain JavaScript in cascade/war_room. Its three existing regions are room-panels (context), war-room-board (board), and side-panels (utilities). Change the layout and interaction layer around those regions without moving their ownership or changing the board's epic/feature/task lens semantics. Desktop reading order and keyboard navigation must follow the visible left-to-right order. At narrow widths, use a clear stacked layout with the board prominent.

Persist panel widths as a presentation preference scoped to this browser and page, with versioned or validated values so stale or impossible widths fall back to defaults. Clamp widths when the viewport changes. Resizing must not mutate board data or fight the 3-second board polling render.

Feature priority is shared domain state, keyed by parent epic and feature ID, not a browser preference. Add a guarded, atomic War Room reorder command and project its canonical order into GET /api/board. Accept an explicit ordered list or move intent only for features still in the same backlog epic, validate membership and concurrency against the current board, and return the accepted canonical order. New backlog features append after ranked peers; missing or departed features are ignored/compacted on read. Keep existing feature dependency/readiness and explicit dispatch rules unchanged. The board's feature lens consumes this order without sorting again by ID.

The performance work measures navigation to first usable board, board API time, render cost, and action-to-visible-update on a representative local board. Optimize the slow path found by measurement, including backend work repeated on every poll and unnecessary full DOM replacement if those are significant. Preserve fresh lifecycle status and current polling/error behavior.

## Cross-module constraints

- Board/feature state and order must be resolved from the same current merged board snapshot used by the War Room. Writes require the usual process and storage guards; do not edit feature docs solely to express a visual reorder.
- Reordering changes priority display only. It must not bypass dependencies, plan approval, execution caps, or trigger feature dispatch. Boss dispatchable feature presentation may use the same order where it shows a queue.
- Existing row actions, selected epic/feature lens, collapsed completed columns, return-to-backlog flow, chat, and sidebar actions must continue to work after layout or rerender changes.
- Provide a non-drag way to move a focused backlog feature up or down, with clear accessible labels and focus retention. Do not let a drag starting on row action controls invoke a row action.
- Avoid extra network requests or expensive work per poll merely to maintain layout preferences or priority order. Failures should retain the last confirmed server order and report the problem to the user.

## Core dependencies

- Existing War Room template, war_room.css, war_room.js, board_focus.js, GET /api/board serialization, and board state/merge snapshot APIs.
- The priority command needs a durable store and validation under the same concurrency conventions used by War Room mutations. Its exact persistence module is an implementation choice for the feature architect as long as it is shared across clients and survives restarts.
- Performance review needs a repeatable local seed/fixture and browser timing plus server timing; use the same fixture before and after. Do not set a target based on network or third-party services outside this app.

## Feature breakdown

- **feat_023_001 — Centered responsive War Room layout and resizable panels.** Put context left, board center, utilities right; use the viewport; add clamped, persistent resize controls and reset; reflow at tablet/mobile widths. Acceptance: wide, medium, and narrow viewport checks; no width jump during board poll, selection, or completed-column expansion; controls remain accessible.
- **feat_023_002 — Durable backlog feature priority.** Add canonical per-epic order and a guarded reorder API; render ordered backlog feature cards with drag/drop and keyboard move controls; keep it coherent after feature creation, dispatch, cancellation, refresh, and concurrent edits. Acceptance: ordering survives reload and another client, is limited to backlog peers in one epic, and stale/invalid writes are refused visibly. Can proceed in parallel with feat_023_001.
- **feat_023_003 — War Room latency review and targeted fixes.** Establish a repeatable baseline, identify the dominant board load and refresh costs, fix the material causes, and record before/after timings. Acceptance: p95 navigation-to-usable-board under 2 seconds on the documented local fixture and machine class across at least 20 runs; no regression in action feedback or lifecycle freshness. Run after feat_023_001 and feat_023_002; compare against a reproducible pre-change revision of the same local fixture.

## Open questions

None blocking. The feature architecture will choose the priority persistence format and concurrency token within the contract above. If the measured 2-second target requires a broader data-path change, propose a scoped amendment with the baseline evidence before changing the target.

## Decision log

- 2026-10-23 · Human · Brief approved through merge request review.

- `dec_001` · 2026-11-05 · Epic Manager · **Feature breakdown**
  Chose Backlog feature priority is a durable order scoped to one epic; reordering changes presentation and queue order but does not trigger or bypass dispatch.
  Rationale: The request asks users to prioritize backlog features. Shared durable order makes that priority consistent across refreshes and clients, while existing dependency and human dispatch controls retain their meaning.
  Honors: Intent and success criteria for backlog drag and drop.

- `dec_002` · 2026-11-05 · Epic Manager · **Macro-architecture**
  Chose Use a desktop context-board-utilities layout with browser-scoped resizable panel widths and responsive fallback.
  Rationale: This directly addresses the unstable board width and varied screen sizes without adding shared layout state or changing board selection behavior.
  Honors: Intent and success criteria for layout, resizing, and screen sizes.

- `dec_003` · 2026-11-05 · Epic Manager · **Core dependencies**
  Chose Measure the existing War Room path before changing it and verify p95 navigation-to-usable-board below 2 seconds on a documented local fixture after the UI features land.
  Rationale: The brief explicitly requests a performance review and a less-than-2-second page load; a shared fixture and before/after measurements make that goal testable without speculative optimization.
  Honors: Intent and success criteria for low latency and page load.

# Edit brief

## Intent

Give the human an Edit action on a backlog epic brief. They can change all brief-authoring fields, including agent assignments and reasoning, submit a new PR/MR for review, and see the merged revision on the same board item and plan view.

### Success criteria

1. Every eligible backlog epic brief exposes Edit. Opening it loads persisted content and assignments from the selected brief; it does not substitute new-brief defaults.
2. Editable fields include title, intent, success criteria, constraints, provider, and model/reasoning selections for all five existing roles: epic_manager, epic_architect, feature_lead, feature_architect, and swe. Other human-authored Markdown sections remain editable and round-trip without loss. “All fields” means brief-authoring content; ID, lifecycle, graph bookkeeping, approval history and runtime metadata remain system-managed.
3. A valid changed submission creates a new PR/MR against the configured product trunk and shows its link. The diff modifies only the existing brief, preserving its ID, path, creation metadata, untouched sections and unrelated metadata. Renaming the title does not allocate a new epic or rename the file.
4. Provider/model/reasoning validation follows the existing brief contract. Saved selections remain visible even when no longer available; validation must not silently change them. Reasoning overrides can be cleared explicitly. Cancel, no-op, and validation failure create no PR and leave approved content unchanged.
5. Submission checks the source brief revision and current backlog eligibility after fetching remote trunk. A changed, missing or activated target produces an actionable reload/conflict response instead of overwriting it. Unrelated trunk commits alone do not make an unchanged brief stale.
6. Before merge, the board continues to show approved content. After merge, the existing automatic sync cadence or forced refresh updates the same row and plan view, including title and agent selections, without duplicating the epic. This works for snapshot-only briefs and for briefs with stale local backlog copies.
7. Activation after refresh uses the approved revision displayed by the board. Local active/completed or live integration state remains authoritative, including when an edit PR merges after activation. Sync failure preserves the last valid view; refresh never resets, checks out, stashes or rebases operator or active worktrees.

## Macro-architecture

Deliver one vertical feature across the existing brief editor, Git-backed PR creation and backlog synchronization.

- **Editor and API:** Reuse the War Room brief dialog and provider/model/reasoning controls. Add an edit mode that retrieves the existing document plus source revision, submits changes for the selected epic, and retains form input on errors. Reuse the existing HTTP, validation and error conventions. Disable repeat submission while a request is in flight and distinguish PR creation from merge/board refresh.
- **Document update and review:** Extend the existing brief service and Git/forge helpers. Resolve the target by epic ID from the configured remote product trunk; use an isolated branch/worktree with a unique edit branch. Patch existing authoring content rather than rebuilding it with the creation template. Preserve non-edited Markdown/frontmatter. Verify the loaded document revision and lifecycle eligibility before committing; return a PR/MR link only when creation actually succeeds.
- **Merged content and activation:** Reuse the remote backlog snapshot and current polling/forced-refresh paths. Current snapshot import omits every local epic ID, merged-board precedence favors local copies, and activation source resolution prefers local HEAD. Narrowly extend these contracts so a validated merged revision of an eligible backlog brief is authoritative over a stale local backlog copy for board reads, plan reads and activation provenance. Preserve local/live lifecycle authority and diagnose genuine unmerged local-content conflicts rather than silently discarding them.

No new service, provider integration, polling loop, generic document editor framework or branch reconciliation system is required. Exact route names and editor presentation belong to feature design; the end-to-end contract above is fixed.

## Cross-module constraints

- PR review/merge remains the approval boundary for edited brief content; edit submission does not activate the epic or overwrite the approved local document.
- Backend eligibility checks are mandatory even when the UI hides Edit for non-backlog work. Recheck eligibility before creating the change. Existing forge review/conflict handling governs later trunk changes while a PR is open.
- Existing inventory validation and five-role semantics remain shared with creation. Never reset existing selections merely because defaults or inventory changed.
- Preserve stable epic identity, original document path, creation date, untouched Markdown and unrelated metadata. Do not reconstruct an existing brief from a blank template or silently drop unrecognized sections.
- Board rows, plan details, edit prefill and activation must agree on source content and provenance. Cache invalidation must allow a merged edit to become visible even when no new epic IDs were imported.
- Remote approved backlog may supersede only stale backlog content. Active/completed lifecycle state and live integration work are never replaced by remote backlog. Detect genuine local unpublished-content conflicts and retain the authoritative local view with diagnostics.
- Git/forge errors must be visible and leave entered values recoverable. If push succeeds but PR creation fails, identify the recoverable branch/state; do not claim a PR was created. General resumable PR management is outside scope.
- Preserve current configured remote/product-trunk resolution, polling behavior, authentication and human activation gate. No destructive operator-checkout operations.

## Core dependencies

- `cascade/briefs.py` and `cascade/brief_stack.py`: creation, persisted assignments and shared inventory validation.
- `cascade/war_room/server.py`, the existing brief dialog, `war_room.js` and `brief_defaults_ui.js`: edit affordance, prefill and submit flow.
- `cascade/tracking.py` and product-trunk resolution: isolated Git changes and supported forge PR/MR creation.
- `cascade/automation.py`, `cascade/workspace/backlog_snapshot.py`, `cascade/workspace/integration_worktree.py`, document routing and activation provenance: coherent approved content.
- Existing brief, API/UI and remote-backlog integration test fixtures. No new external dependency.

## Feature breakdown

1. **feat_024_001 — Edit backlog briefs through PRs and refresh approved content**
   - Deliver the Edit action, complete authoring-field prefill/editing, shared validation and conflict handling.
   - Create the isolated one-brief PR/MR while preserving document identity and content.
   - Make merged edits visible in board/plan reads and use that revision for activation.
   - Verify the full edit → PR diff → merge → refresh → activation-source path.

This is one shippable slice: an edit that creates a PR but leaves the board or activation stale does not meet the user intent. The feature team may sequence internal tasks; there are no sibling feature dependencies.

### Validation and delivery boundary

Prefer one integration scenario using real local Git repositories with the forge boundary faked: edit all authoring fields on a document containing extra Markdown, inspect the one-file diff, merge upstream, refresh, and verify the same board ID, plan content, assignments and activation source. Include stale local backlog and diverged operator checkout conditions. Add focused API/UI checks for prefill, clearing reasoning, invalid selections, no-op/cancel, stale revision, non-backlog rejection and submission failure recovery. Preserve create-brief regression coverage. Do not duplicate integration coverage with broad mock-heavy unit suites.

Out of scope: editing active/completed plans through this flow, automatic merging or activation, generic lifecycle/YAML editing, adding agent roles/providers, pending-PR dashboards, and general merge-conflict management.

## Open questions

No unresolved product-scope questions block feature planning. The feature design must settle the following implementation choices within this contract:

- Choose a lossless way to edit the supported Markdown sections and expose other author-authored sections; irregular documents must not be silently normalized or truncated.
- Define the source revision token and stale-local-versus-unpublished-local comparison. Cover snapshot-only and locally present backlog briefs consistently across reads and activation.
- Verify the eligibility/activation race and push-success/PR-failure recovery using existing infrastructure. A late merged edit must never overwrite active work.

## Decision log

- 2026-10-25 · Human · Brief approved through merge request review.

- `dec_001` · 2026-10-25 · Epic Manager · **Scope and delivery**
  Chose Deliver one vertical feature, feat_024_001, for backlog brief authoring-field edits, a new PR/MR, and post-merge board/plan/activation coherence. Keep identity and lifecycle metadata system-managed; preserve the existing path and untouched content..
  Rationale: The user outcome is incomplete if an edit PR exists but the board or subsequent activation still uses the old brief. Reusing the existing brief form, validation and Git/forge flow minimizes scope while supporting every existing authoring field and additional human-authored Markdown.
  Honors: Edit button; all brief-authoring fields including all five role models and reasoning; new review PR; updated board; frugal engineering and stable epic identity..

- `dec_002` · 2026-10-25 · Epic Manager · **Approved backlog content and provenance**
  Chose Extend backlog precedence narrowly so merged remote brief revisions supersede stale local backlog copies consistently for board, plan and activation; retain active/completed/live-worktree authority and diagnose unpublished local-content conflicts..
  Rationale: Current snapshot import omits every local epic ID and activation prefers local HEAD. Leaving those rules unchanged would hide merged edits or activate an older brief. The correction must not mutate operator checkouts or overwrite in-flight lifecycle state.
  Honors: Board updates after merge; same epic identity; approved source provenance; existing sync cadence and human activation gate; protection of active work..

# Recover failed work item actions

## Intent

When a user or team requests an action on an epic, feature, or task, Cascade should complete it or repair a recoverable failure without asking the user to run Git commands or clean a checkout. The initiating action remains pending while recovery runs, then finishes or reports a precise blocker. In particular, closing an epic must work when the operator's product trunk checkout has unrelated tracked or untracked changes.

### Success criteria

- A failed action carries a typed reason, affected work item, owning checkout or branch, retry state, and safe next step. The War Room shows that recovery is underway and the eventual result; it does not turn a recoverable first failure into a terminal refusal.
- The supervisor handles deterministic task failures and repository mechanics with scoped operations. It can retry or resume the existing Task run, repair a missing integration checkout, use an isolated checkout for trunk operations, and retry a merge after its preconditions are restored.
- The Feature Team handles task decisions requiring code or feature-plan judgment; the Epic Team handles cross-feature and epic-plan decisions. Parent teams can request recovery, while the supervisor owns scheduling, locks, and execution.
- Epic close succeeds with a dirty operator trunk by using the existing reviewed-branch and isolated closeout-review path. It never commits, stashes, resets, cleans, or merges unrelated operator changes. A merged implementation review and terminal closeout review are verified before completion is recorded.
- Safe recovery preserves action identity and authorization: retries are bounded, durable, idempotent, serialized with lifecycle mutations, and resume after supervisor restart without duplicate turns, reviews, merges, or completion events.
- Missing credentials, unavailable services, insufficient permissions, human review gates, ambiguous semantic conflicts, and unrelated dirty integration files become explicit blockers with ownership and a retry path. Recovery does not grant broader permissions or bypass a human decision.

## Macro-architecture

Introduce a shared action-recovery boundary around epic, feature, and task lifecycle actions. Persist the requested action and recovery state, classify failures from existing typed lifecycle results, and choose a bounded remedy. Retry the original action only after re-reading current board, branch, review, lease, and permission state under the lifecycle lock.

The supervisor is the coordinator and privileged executor for deterministic Git and Task-run repairs. Parent teams receive scoped recovery requests only when a remedy requires code or plan judgment. A semantic task conflict is handed to the Feature Team; a cross-feature or epic-contract conflict is handed to the Epic Team. The same persisted action resumes after that team records a resolution.

For trunk operations, use a clean temporary worktree based on the verified remote product trunk and open or reuse the normal review. For integration worktree changes, preserve local files and return work to the owning agent when validation or semantic conflict resolution is needed. Record every attempt and outcome in action history. The War Room exposes pending, repairing, awaiting decision or review, blocked, and completed states, with one retry control for terminal blockers after the underlying condition changes.

## Cross-module constraints

- Preserve all user and agent changes. Never automatically discard, reset, clean, force-push, or stash a checkout. Do not absorb unrelated files into an action commit or review.
- Respect existing human approval, comment, review, and authorization gates. The original request authorizes bounded retries of that action, but not merging an unreviewed change or changing credentials and permissions.
- Keep Task workers' current Git and forge permissions unchanged. Deterministic recovery belongs to the supervisor's existing privileged execution boundary.
- Prevent loops with a configurable attempt limit, backoff for transient failures, and a terminal typed blocker. Serialize user, team, and automatic recovery requests for the same action.
- Reuse branch synchronization, integration worktrees, Task execution and merge queues, review tracking, and existing lifecycle event contracts. Keep branch provenance and the selected review target stable.
- Do not build a generic workflow engine, arbitrary rollback, or automatic semantic conflict resolver in this epic.

## Core dependencies

- Existing supervisor, Task execution lease, checkpoint, and pending merge queue.
- Epic, feature, and task lifecycle actions and their typed failure results.
- Integration worktree and branch synchronization services.
- Review tracking and forge authentication for review creation and verification.
- War Room action routes, status model, and recovery controls.

## Feature breakdown
- feat_026_001
- feat_026_002
- feat_026_003
- feat_026_004

1. **Durable action recovery state**
   - Add a stable action identity and persisted recovery state around lifecycle actions.
   - Classify existing failures into deterministic repair, transient retry, owner decision, human gate, and terminal blocker.
   - Enforce serialization, bounded attempts, idempotent resumption after restart, and attempt history.
   - Acceptance: restart and concurrent-retry integration tests prove one logical action produces no duplicate team turns, reviews, merges, or completion events.

2. **Supervisor repair and owning-team handoff**
   - Implement only deterministic remedies needed by current lifecycle failures: resume an interrupted Task run, restore a missing integration checkout, and retry a queued merge after mechanical preconditions recover.
   - Route semantic task/code conflicts to the Feature Team and cross-feature or epic-contract conflicts to the Epic Team, including action context and a resume token/reference.
   - Acceptance: interrupted Task and feature merge-conflict scenarios either resume to completion or enter the correct owned decision state without widening worker permissions.

3. **War Room recovery feedback and retry**
   - Show recovery phase, typed reason, attempt count, owning actor, affected checkout or branch, and next safe step on the original action.
   - Provide a single retry control only for retryable terminal blockers; keep approval and review gates distinct.
   - Acceptance: transient forge failure, permission refusal, and concurrent retry scenarios display the correct state and produce at most one resumed execution.

4. **Dirty-trunk-safe epic close**
   - Run trunk-dependent closeout work in an isolated checkout based on verified remote product trunk.
   - Reuse or open the normal closeout review, verify the implementation review is merged and terminal closeout review is satisfied, then resume the original close action.
   - Acceptance: an epic closes while the operator trunk contains unrelated tracked and untracked files; those files and the operator checkout remain byte-for-byte and index-state unchanged.

## Delivery order

Deliver features 1 and 2 first because all recovery paths depend on durable identity and ownership. Features 3 and 4 may then proceed in parallel: Feature 3 exposes the established state model without creating a second orchestration path, while Feature 4 applies the boundary to the initiating dirty-trunk defect.

## Open questions

_(none)_

## Decision log

- 2026-10-26 · Human · Brief proposed for review after epic_009 close exposed a dirty product trunk checkout.
- 2026-10-26 · Epic Manager · Keep Task worker permissions unchanged; place deterministic recovery in the supervisor boundary.
- 2026-10-26 · Epic Manager · Route semantic task/code conflicts to the Feature Team and cross-feature or epic-contract conflicts to the Epic Team; resume the original persisted action after resolution.
- 2026-10-26 · Epic Manager · Limit the epic to current lifecycle recovery paths; exclude a generic workflow engine, arbitrary rollback, and automatic semantic conflict resolution.

- `dec_001` · 2026-10-26 · Epic Manager · **Cross-module constraints**
  Chose Keep Task worker permissions unchanged; deterministic recovery runs inside the supervisor's existing privileged execution boundary..
  Rationale: Routine checkout, lease, and merge-queue repair does not require product judgment and must not broaden worker authority.
  Honors: Success criteria requiring scoped supervisor repair without broader permissions..

- `dec_002` · 2026-10-26 · Epic Manager · **Macro-architecture**
  Chose Route semantic task/code conflicts to the Feature Team and cross-feature or epic-contract conflicts to the Epic Team, then resume the same persisted action after resolution..
  Rationale: The owning planning level should decide semantics while the supervisor retains scheduling, locking, and execution.
  Honors: The ownership model and action-identity requirements in the epic intent..

- `dec_003` · 2026-10-26 · Epic Manager · **Cross-module constraints**
  Chose Exclude a generic workflow engine, arbitrary rollback, and automatic semantic conflict resolution..
  Rationale: These additions are not necessary to recover the known lifecycle failures and would materially expand cost and risk.
  Honors: The smallest shippable slice for reliable action recovery..
## Amendment log

- 2026-10-26 · Epic Architect · Corrected the Feature 3/4 numbering to match the minted IDs: feat_026_003 is War Room recovery feedback and retry; feat_026_004 is dirty-trunk-safe epic close. No scope or architecture changed.

# Recover orphaned Task deliveries

## Intent

The Feature Team should detect and recover an active child Task whose worker has stopped before delivery finishes. A green test result must not make the Task appear ready to merge until a validated deliverable commit and durable merge queue entry exist. Recovery should finish the existing Task or resume its worker without a human editing Git or runtime state.

Task `task_026_002_004` exposed the gap: the ready toast preceded its commit, execution remained `awaiting_merge` with no live owner or pending merge, and the existing parent health sweep treated it as healthy. The earlier draft in `docs/briefs/parent_team_task_recovery.md` describes the same interrupted-delivery case.

### Success criteria

- The parent health sweep compares Task status and execution phase with owner lease, worktree, deliverable commit, validation evidence, and merge queue. An active Task with no live owner and no pending or completed merge is `recovery_needed`, including when its stored phase says `awaiting_merge`.
- Set `awaiting_merge` and emit the ready toast only after a matching validated commit and durable merge request are recorded. A passing test alone remains validation evidence, tied to the tree it tested.
- The supervisor performs one serialized, durable recovery decision per Task incident. If a valid deliverable commit exists, it requeues the same Task merge. Otherwise it resumes the existing Task branch, worktree, and checkpoint, preserving files and pinned provider, model, skills, Task plan, and Feature plan.
- The owning Feature Team can request `recover_task(task_id)` for a direct child and receives a precise outcome. The periodic sweep and this tool use the same recovery operation; a simultaneous request or supervisor restart cannot spawn two workers or merge twice.
- A live owner, unsafe worktree, changed test tree, missing branch, red tests, and semantic merge conflict yield explicit blockers. Unresolved recovery appears in the parent state and War Room; recovery clears only the derived blocker.

## Delivery contract

A Task becomes merge-ready only in this order:

1. `swe_commit` produces the deliverable commit on the existing Task branch.
2. Final validation runs against that exact commit and records the commit SHA and Feature-base SHA.
3. The durable pending merge request is recorded for the same Task, deliverable SHA, and base SHA.
4. Only then may execution enter `awaiting_merge` and emit the ready notification.

Pre-commit test runs remain useful feedback but never satisfy final delivery validation. If either the deliverable tree or Feature base changes, final validation must run again. This commit-first final validation contract removes the need to infer an exact tested tree from a drained dirty worktree.

## Macro-architecture

Extend the existing supervisor direct-report health sweep and Task lifecycle boundaries. Give the recovery operation a stable Task incident identity and acquire the Task lifecycle lock before rechecking board state, lease, worktree, checkpoint, commit, validation, and queue. Treat a commit with matching final validation as a merge-repair case; treat every other incomplete delivery as a resume case. Reuse the existing pending merge queue, SWE execution, and parent blockage provenance.

Make the commit-to-validation-to-queue transition restart-safe. On a later sweep, reconstruct the correct state from durable evidence instead of trusting the `awaiting_merge` label. Give the Feature Team a scoped recovery tool that requests supervisor action and reports its result; process cancellation and Git mutation remain in the supervisor.

## Cross-module constraints

- Preserve uncommitted work and the existing Task branch. Never reset, clean, stash, force-push, or silently create a replacement branch.
- Do not reuse final validation after the deliverable commit or Feature base changes.
- Do not replace a live owner based only on heartbeat age; cancel a stalled owner within a bound and wait for lease release before resuming.
- Keep retries bounded and idempotent across concurrent sweeps, parent requests, and supervisor restarts. Respect existing ownership, review, and merge-conflict gates.
- Reuse the current health sweep and action-recovery state; avoid a second scheduler or status store.
- Recovery may clear only the blocker provenance created for the same recovery incident.

## Core dependencies

- Task execution lease, checkpoint, worktree registry, `swe_run_tests`, and `swe_commit`.
- Durable pending Task merge queue and normal Task-to-Feature merge path.
- Feature Team tool boundary and supervisor direct-report health sweep.
- Existing parent blockage provenance and War Room status model.

## Feature breakdown
- feat_027_003
- feat_027_002
- feat_027_001

### 1. Enforce the durable Task delivery boundary

Make commit, exact-commit final validation, durable queue insertion, `awaiting_merge`, and ready notification follow the delivery contract. Persist enough evidence to compare Task ID, deliverable SHA, and Feature-base SHA after restart. Cover drains after commit and after validation, changed-tree/base revalidation, red validation, and replay without duplicate queue entries.

### 2. Detect and recover orphaned Task delivery

Extend the direct-report health sweep and shared supervisor recovery operation. Under the Task lifecycle lock, derive a stable incident, recheck live ownership and durable evidence, then either requeue a matching validated commit or resume the existing execution context. Preserve dirty worktrees and pinned execution inputs. Cover drain before commit, drain before queueing, restart replay, live-owner protection, unsafe/missing Git state, bounded cancellation, and concurrent recovery requests.

Depends on Feature 1.

### 3. Expose scoped recovery and recovery state

Add the owning Feature Team's `recover_task(task_id)` request using the same supervisor operation. Return precise outcomes (`not_needed`, `owner_live`, `requeued`, `resumed`, `in_progress`, or `blocked` with reason). Surface unresolved incidents through existing parent blockage provenance and War Room state, including semantic merge conflict, and clear only the matching derived blocker. Cover authorization to direct children, simultaneous tool/sweep requests, outcome rendering, and blocker lifecycle.

Depends on Feature 2.

## Explicit exclusions

- Recovery of non-Task descendants or Tasks owned by another Feature Team.
- A new scheduler, merge queue, status store, replacement branch, or generic Git repair tool.
- Automatic resolution of semantic merge conflicts, red tests, unsafe worktrees, or missing branches.
- Reworking unrelated notification, lease, or checkpoint behavior.

## Open questions

_(none)_

## Decision log

- 2026-10-26 · Human · Brief proposed after Task `task_026_002_004` required a manual merge requeue.

- `dec_001` · 2026-10-31 · Epic Manager · **Delivery contract**
  Chose Require commit-first final validation keyed by Task ID, deliverable commit SHA, and Feature-base SHA before durable merge queue insertion, awaiting_merge, or the ready notification..
  Rationale: A drained dirty worktree has no reliably durable identity. Validating the actual deliverable commit makes restart checks exact and forces revalidation whenever the deliverable or base changes.
  Honors: Success criteria requiring a matching validated commit and durable merge request; smallest restart-safe design without a new artifact system..

- `dec_002` · 2026-10-31 · Epic Manager · **Feature breakdown**
  Chose Sequence three features: durable delivery boundary; orphan detection and recovery; scoped parent control and recovery visibility..
  Rationale: The recovery engine depends on trustworthy durable evidence, while the parent tool and presentation should reuse the proven engine rather than create a parallel path.
  Honors: Ruthless prioritization, shared recovery semantics, and integration ownership with minimal cross-feature coupling..
## Amendment log

_(none)_

# Make epic close reviews visible in the War Room

## Intent

When closing an epic requires an implementation review, the War Room should show a durable, clickable review action on that epic. The operator should be able to follow the review, return after a refresh, and see when closeout has finished without guessing what `pending_close_review` means or searching the forge.

`epic_026` exposed the gap. The close API returned `pending_close_review`, and PR #106 existed, but the UI supplied no usable link. The current close handler writes a review URL into status text when one is returned; `setStatus` uses `textContent`, so that URL is plain text and disappears on refresh. The board view attaches review state to Features but not to Epics.

Epic closure also currently requires two reviews: one to merge the epic implementation branch and another that effectively only moves the epic plan to completed. This epic collapses those steps. The implementation review must include the completed-state plan move, and reconciliation must finish closure from that same review after its merge is verified.

### Success criteria

- Represent the epic close stage explicitly: implementation review pending, completed, or an actionable blocker. Keep the review URL, source and target branches, and forge state with the stage. Reconstruct this state after a service restart; a transient button response is not the only source of truth.
- When `Close epic` opens or finds the implementation review, return its URL in the API response and render an `Open implementation review` link beside the epic's Close action. The link remains on the Epic row after board refresh, navigation, and restart.
- Generate the completed-state epic plan move on the epic implementation branch before opening its review. Do not open a second terminal closeout review after the implementation review merges.
- Keep the original close action pending while the implementation review is open. After it merges, reconcile the same action automatically, or expose a clear `Finish close` action if automatic reconciliation cannot run. Show completion only after the review merge and completed epic document on remote trunk are verified.
- Make `Close epic` idempotent while a review is pending: it reveals the existing review and never creates a second PR.

## Macro-architecture

Extend the existing epic close result, review lookup, board serialization, and War Room Epic row. Before the implementation review is opened, stage the epic document's move to completed in the same branch and commit as the implementation changes. Reuse the normal forge review snapshot and close action reconciliation path as the single authority for pending closure. After merge, verify both the merged review and the completed document on remote trunk, then finalize the close action without creating a terminal review.

The feature review row and backlog cancellation review link are useful UI precedents.

## Cross-module constraints

- Do not merge reviews automatically or change the human review policy.
- Do not modify the operator product-trunk checkout.
- Keep review URLs as validated external links and avoid rendering forge text as HTML.
- Preserve the existing safe external-link component and review registry rather than introducing a separate transient UI status store.
- The completed-state move and implementation changes must share one review; no terminal-only closeout PR may be created.

## Core dependencies

- Existing epic close API and close action reconciliation.
- Forge review lookup and durable review snapshot.
- Epic worktree document lifecycle and remote-trunk verification.
- War Room board serialization and Epic row rendering.

## Feature breakdown
- feat_028_003
- feat_028_002
- feat_028_001

The Epic Team will sequence a smallest shippable slice covering: single-review close preparation and reconciliation; durable pending-review state and API/board exposure; and War Room Epic-row controls. API and browser coverage should exercise the pending stage, failed review lookup, link accessibility, refresh, idempotency, merged-review reconciliation, and completion without a second PR.

## Acceptance scenarios

- Closing a ready epic stages the completed-state plan move with its implementation changes, opens one implementation review, and immediately shows a clickable link on the Epic row.
- Refreshing the page or restarting Cascade retains the review link and pending stage without another Close click.
- Repeated close requests while the review is open reveal the same review and do not create another PR.
- After the implementation review merges, automatic or operator-triggered reconciliation verifies both the merge and completed epic document on remote trunk, moves the epic to completed, and removes the pending review action.
- No terminal closeout review is opened at any point.
- A missing review URL or failed merge/document verification yields a specific actionable blocker rather than a bare `pending_close_review` label.
- API and browser tests cover pending review, missing or failed review lookup, link accessibility, refresh, idempotency, merged-review reconciliation, and completion. The dirty operator checkout stays unchanged throughout.

## Open questions

_(none)_

## Decision log

- 2026-10-30 · Human · Promoted the draft in `docs/briefs/epic_close_review_workflow.md` to the War Room backlog.
- `dec_001` · 2026-11-03 · Human · **Epic closure workflow**
  Chose Use one epic closure review: stage the epic plan's completed-state move in the implementation PR, then verify the merged review and completed remote-trunk document to finalize closure without a terminal-only PR.
  Rationale: The second review carries no independent implementation value; folding the lifecycle move into the implementation review preserves human review while removing redundant closeout ceremony.
  Honors: In reply to: cmt_001.

# Pause work when its provider is unavailable

## Intent

Epic `epic_028` was activated with Cursor pinned for both planning roles. Cursor is not authenticated on this machine, so both roles repeatedly report `provider startup failed` and the epic appears active without a useful plan. Make provider setup failures a clear, durable state with an operator action, for Epic, Feature, and Task starts. The operator must be able to select another available provider and suitable models for the affected work item, including after activation, without obtaining credentials for a provider they intentionally stopped using.

### Success criteria

- Before activating an Epic or dispatching a Feature or Task, check the effective pinned provider and role models against installed/authenticated provider capability. On a deterministic setup failure, leave the item in its prior column, create no new worktree or checkpoint, and return a structured reason and next step to the War Room. Recheck at the execution boundary because provider availability can change after preflight.
- Include the selected service tier, including flex mode, in that capability check. If the provider rejects the tier only when a turn starts, record an actionable unsupported-tier blocker and stop repeating the same failed turn. Offer a human choice to disable flex or select another supported provider and model; never silently switch to a tier with different cost or latency.
- If credentials or provider availability disappear after work has started, pause further starts for that work item and persist one provider-blocked incident with the work ID, affected roles, provider, safe reason, last attempt, and recommended remedy. Show it on the board and in the room after refresh and restart; never expose credential values or raw provider payloads.
- Show a human-only `Change provider` action on provider-blocked Epic, Feature, and Task rows, including items already in `2_active`. The War Room shows the current provider and per-role models, offers installed/authenticated replacement providers and their supported models, and validates every affected role before submission. Keep a saved unavailable selection visible; do not require the old provider to be authenticated to replace it. For a backlog Epic, this action may open the existing reviewed brief editor; an active item must have a direct recovery path without first returning to backlog.
- Apply an active-item provider change through one serialized, durable recovery operation. Stop or wait for any in-flight turn, recheck ownership and lifecycle gates, record the human's provider/model selection and audit provenance, and reconcile document/runtime settings with checkpoint-pinned provider, model, reasoning, and flex choices before any turn resumes. A restart or partial failure must leave either the old blocked selection or a fully applied new selection, never a checkpoint that silently invokes the old provider. Preserve the reviewed plan, approval state, branch, worktree, transcript, and dirty files. Existing child items retain their own selections; clearly show which future role defaults on the selected item will change.
- Treat provider-neutral progress as durable context, but never rewrite or resume opaque provider-specific turn state under a different provider. If checkpoint compatibility cannot be proven, create a fresh role turn from the preserved plan, progress summary, and existing worktree after the new selection commits atomically.
- After a successful change, offer or start one safe retry on the same work item using the new provider. Resume a compatible checkpoint; when provider-specific turn state cannot be reused, start a fresh role turn with the preserved plan, prior progress, and worktree context. Never reset files, duplicate work, bypass approval/review gates, or treat a provider change as permission to rerun an already completed action. If safe migration is impossible, keep the item blocked with a precise reason and next step.
- Also offer a human retry with the original provider after its setup is repaired. Retry and provider change must be idempotent under concurrent clicks and watchdog ticks and avoid duplicate agent turns or repeated failure toasts. Transient transport failures may use bounded backoff; missing authentication or invalid configuration waits for an explicit change or retry.
- Keep provider selection pinned until a human changes it. Do not silently fall back to another provider or model. Show provider setup, Change provider, and, for an eligible unstarted Epic, Return to backlog as distinct remedies.
- API, board, browser, restart, and lifecycle tests cover missing credential at activation, provider loss after activation, Cursor-to-Codex recovery of an active Epic such as `epic_028`, active Feature and dirty Task migration, stale checkpoint pins, concurrent change/retry requests, restored original credentials, refusal with an in-flight turn that cannot be stopped, and unaffected sibling or child work.

## Macro-architecture

Reuse the effective backend resolver and provider inventory for read-only eligibility and model choices. A human-only recovery command owns the provider change and coordinates lifecycle locks, turn quiescence, durable selection provenance, checkpoint reconciliation, and the normal kickoff/retry path. The board projects the current effective selection and provider-blocked state so the controls survive refresh and restart.

## Cross-module constraints

Reuse provider probes, credential resolution, role/model selection, checkpoint recovery, and the existing War Room health/recovery presentation. Keep startup checks read-only until dispatch is authorized. Treat a human-approved provider change as an explicit operational override, not an edit to reviewed plan prose or an automatic rewrite of child work. Preserve dirty work and prior selection history. Never log secrets, auto-switch providers, require credentials for the abandoned provider, or let a failed provider stall the supervisor or unrelated work.

## Core dependencies

- Existing provider inventory and credential probes, War Room provider/model controls, and model resolution.
- Epic, Feature, and Task checkpoints with pinned role backends, lifecycle locks, and normal kickoff/retry paths.
- Existing backlog brief editor for reviewed edits before activation; Return to backlog remains a separate action for unstarted Epics.

## Feature breakdown
- feat_029_003
- feat_029_002
- feat_029_001

1. **Provider preflight and durable blocker state.** Add the shared capability check at Epic activation and Feature/Task dispatch, execution-boundary recheck, deterministic-versus-transient failure handling, and one restart-safe provider-blocked incident per work item.
2. **Atomic active-item provider recovery.** Add one human-authorized command for Epic, Feature, and Task that serializes against lifecycle activity, validates all affected role selections and tier settings, commits selection plus checkpoint reconciliation atomically, preserves provider-neutral work, and chooses compatible resume or fresh-turn reconstruction.
3. **War Room recovery controls and lifecycle proof.** Project blocked state and safe reasons, expose Change provider and Retry with distinct remedies, and cover the end-to-end browser/API/restart/concurrency cases. Reuse existing provider/model selectors rather than creating a parallel settings flow.

Sequence 1 before 2; feature 3 may build its read-only presentation against feature 1 but its mutating controls depend on feature 2.

## Open questions

_(none)_

## Decision log

- 2026-10-31 · Human · Brief approved through merge request review.

- `dec_001` · 2026-11-02 · Epic Manager · **Checkpoint recovery contract**
  Chose Preserve provider-neutral progress, but do not rewrite or resume opaque provider-specific turn state under a different provider; when compatibility is not provable, atomically commit the new selection and reconstruct a fresh role turn from the preserved plan, progress, and worktree..
  Rationale: This makes the smallest safe recovery behavior explicit, prevents stale checkpoints from invoking the abandoned provider, and preserves user work without requiring provider-specific migration support.
  Honors: Human-approved provider pinning, atomic recovery, dirty-work preservation, and no silent fallback..

# Return an unstarted Epic to backlog

## Intent

An Epic can be activated before its pinned provider proves usable. `epic_028` is active with Cursor, but planning cannot proceed because Cursor is not authenticated. Give an operator a safe, human-only **Return to backlog** action for an active Epic and its full descendant graph, so the approved brief can be revised through the existing reviewed backlog-edit flow and the same Epic, Features, and Tasks can later be reactivated with corrected provider/model choices and an explicit freshness review.

This is a lifecycle correction, not cancellation, plan reset, or an in-place provider edit.

### Success criteria

- Show **Return to backlog** on an active Epic when the shared eligibility evaluator proves the Epic and its complete descendant graph can be preserved and transitioned without data loss. Existing children, approved plans, and review history are not disqualifiers; missing graph provenance, unsafe in-flight work, or unpreservable Git state are. Every failed condition is surfaced on the Epic row.
- On request, quiesce all in-flight turns in the Epic descendant graph, acquire lifecycle locks for the graph in deterministic order, and re-evaluate eligibility under those locks before mutation.
- Execute a durable, restart-safe, idempotent transition with one audit event. Retries return the recorded result and never duplicate checkpoints, branches, worktrees, backlog briefs, or events.
- Move the same Epic and every descendant to backlog as one graph-preserving operation, remove their active board pointers, and expose the Epic's existing MR-backed backlog editor.
- Preserve or archive the former integration branch, worktree, transcripts, and startup-failure evidence. Refuse when dirty files or unmerged commits cannot be preserved without loss. Never reset or switch the operator trunk.
- After an approved provider/model edit merges and backlog refresh completes, reactivation restores the descendant graph, creates fresh run identities and role pins, ignores obsolete checkpoints, and requires each owning agent team to review its plan for staleness before work resumes.
- End-to-end coverage includes the `epic_028` missing-credential shape, concurrent/repeated requests, restart between transition steps, all material refusal cases, reviewed provider editing, and successful Codex reactivation.

## Scope

### In scope

- A human-only API/command and War Room row control for active Epic graph → backlog.
- A single shared, structured eligibility evaluator used for presentation and command enforcement.
- Quiescence, lifecycle locking, durable transition journaling, recovery, idempotency, and audit emission.
- Restoration of the approved source brief through existing backlog storage/refresh behavior.
- Preservation of Epic and descendant artifacts, graph relationships, and history, with invalidation of stale activation state.
- Reuse of the existing reviewed backlog-brief edit and activation flows.

### Out of scope

- Independently returning a Feature or Task while its Epic remains active.
- Destructive rollback, deletion, or erasure of approved plans, child work, review activity, or substantive edits.
- Editing provider/model pins directly on an active Epic.
- Automatic provider fallback, automatic MR creation/merge, cancellation, destructive cleanup, branch deletion, or trunk manipulation.
- A general-purpose lifecycle migration framework beyond the minimum durable transition required here.

## Eligibility contract

Eligibility is evaluated from authoritative persisted state, not UI state. The evaluator returns `eligible` plus stable reason codes and operator-readable explanations.

An Epic is eligible only when all of the following hold:

1. It is currently an active Epic and is not already in another terminal or lifecycle transition.
2. Its complete descendant graph can be enumerated from authoritative state, with stable IDs, parent links, source revisions, approvals, comments, and review history sufficient for deterministic restoration.
3. Every in-flight turn in the graph can be quiesced, and no graph member is already in a conflicting terminal or lifecycle transition.
4. Every Epic/Feature/Task plan, review artifact, amendment, checkpoint, and substantive change can be preserved as history; their existence is not a refusal condition.
5. Every graph member's branch/worktree state can be preserved or archived without data loss. Dirty files or unmerged commits are allowed only when the retention mechanism can prove they remain reachable and restorable.
6. Required Epic source brief, activation provenance, and descendant activation provenance exist so the same graph can be restored deterministically.
7. A deterministic lifecycle-lock order is available for the complete graph.
8. No conflicting lifecycle operation is in progress.

The evaluator must identify every failing condition in one response. The command must run the same evaluator again after quiescence and while holding the lifecycle lock; a stale UI result never authorizes the transition.

## Macro-architecture

### 1. Shared eligibility and presentation

Add a read-only domain service for return eligibility. It consumes the Epic lifecycle record, the complete descendant graph, activation/source references, planning and review state, checkpoints/turn outcomes, and Git status for every graph member. It emits stable reason codes suitable for API clients and a human explanation for each refusal.

Both the API command and War Room row use this service. The row displays the action only to authorized humans for active Epics; when unavailable, it displays the refusal explanation(s) rather than silently hiding the capability.

Approved or substantively changed plans do not block return; they become preserved review inputs. Eligibility is about lossless graph transition and deterministic restoration, not whether work has occurred. Do not infer safety from timestamps or provider-failure status alone.

### 2. Lifecycle command and durable transition

Implement a human-authorized `return_epic_to_backlog(epic_id, request_id)` application command:

1. Resolve an existing completed/in-progress operation by idempotency key or Epic transition record.
2. Resolve the complete descendant graph, request quiescence for every owning team, and wait until no role turn in the graph can still commit state.
3. Acquire lifecycle locks for the Epic and descendants in deterministic graph order.
4. Re-read authoritative state, re-resolve the graph, and re-run the eligibility evaluator; abort if membership changed.
5. Create or resume a durable transition journal keyed by Epic ID with ordered steps and captured source/active provenance.
6. Preserve/archive all graph-member plans, branches, worktrees, transcripts, reviews, comments, diagnostics, and checkpoints without deleting history.
7. Restore/upsert the Epic backlog brief and persist a graph manifest containing descendant identities, relationships, revisions, and prior lifecycle states.
8. Invalidate active-run identities and role pins, remove active board pointers for the whole graph, and atomically publish the graph in backlog state.
9. Commit the lifecycle result and emit exactly one audit event through an outbox/deduplicated event key.

Each step is replay-safe and records completion before advancing. Recovery resumes the journal after process restart. Concurrent requests serialize on the lifecycle lock and converge on the same completed outcome. A request arriving after success reports the recorded success.

No step resets, checks out, or force-updates operator trunk. Failure before commit leaves the Epic visibly active or explicitly transition-pending; it must never present two independently editable authoritative copies.

### 3. Existing backlog edit and fresh activation

The restored item is a normal backlog brief and uses the existing MR-backed editor, approval, merge, and backlog refresh path. This Epic adds no bypass for active-plan metadata.

A later Epic activation reads the newly approved backlog revision and graph manifest, restores all descendants and relationships, creates fresh activation/run identities, and resolves fresh provider/model role pins. Before any resumed implementation, each owning Epic or Feature agent team reviews its restored plan against the revised ancestor contract and records any required amendment or a fresh sign-off. Checkpoint lookup is scoped to the new activation/run identity, so archived runs cannot silently resume. Old artifacts remain evidence and review inputs, not executable activation state.

## State and invariants

- Epic and descendant IDs, graph relationships, approved plans, source history, comments, reviews, and audit history remain stable across the transition.
- Exactly one graph state is authoritative: all members remain active/transition-pending until commit, then all are backlog; partial publication is forbidden.
- A completed transition has one durable result and one audit event.
- Archived run artifacts are evidence and freshness-review inputs, not resumable execution state.
- Refusal is side-effect free except for normal observability.
- Eligibility reason codes are part of the API contract and are shared with the War Room.
- If safety cannot be proven, refuse and explain; never attempt cleanup to manufacture eligibility.

## Cross-module constraints

- Human approval remains required for changing an approved brief; reuse the existing MR-backed backlog edit path.
- Preserve IDs, comments, source revision provenance, and history.
- Do not cancel completed/reviewed work, delete or rewrite dirty artifacts, force-push, or bypass provider, authorization, freshness review, or lifecycle gates.
- Graph-wide quiescence must prevent any descendant role turn from committing after the locked eligibility check.
- Lock ordering must follow existing lifecycle conventions; do not hold the lifecycle lock while waiting for a turn to stop.
- Board refresh and audit delivery may be retried; both must be deduplicated from durable transition identity.
- Failure messages must be actionable without exposing credentials or transcript secrets.

## Core dependencies

- Epic/Feature/Task lifecycle state machines and deterministic multi-entity lifecycle locking.
- Epic and descendant team scheduler/quiescence mechanisms.
- Plan approval/sign-off, child graph, review/amendment, and checkpoint stores.
- Activation provenance and approved backlog brief storage.
- Integration branch/worktree Git inspection and artifact retention.
- Existing backlog MR editor, merge/refresh pipeline, and activation pin resolver.
- Board/War Room API, authorization, audit event/outbox, and recovery runner.

## Feature breakdown
- feat_030_003
- feat_030_002
- feat_030_001

### Feature 1 — Eligibility contract and operator control

Deliver the shared eligibility evaluator, stable refusal reasons, human authorization, API read/command contract, and War Room row behavior. Include focused domain tests for every predicate and an integration test proving presentation and command use identical results.

This feature establishes the safety contract but does not mutate lifecycle state independently of Feature 2.

### Feature 2 — Durable, idempotent active-to-backlog transition

Deliver graph-wide quiescence, deterministic multi-entity locking, locked graph recheck, transition journal, graph manifest and artifact preservation, atomic backlog publication, active-pointer removal, stale-run invalidation, recovery, and exactly-once audit semantics.

High-signal tests cover two concurrent requests, repeated requests after success, graph membership races, injected restart/failure at each durable boundary, descendant turns racing with quiescence, preservable and unpreservable dirty/unmerged Git cases, atomic graph publication, and evidence preservation without operator-trunk changes.

Depends on Feature 1.

### Feature 3 — Reviewed edit and clean reactivation journey

Wire the restored Epic into the existing MR-backed brief editor and verify activation restores the descendant graph with fresh run identities and role pins, then gates resumed work on agent-team freshness review.

One end-to-end scenario models an Epic with approved child Features: return the full graph → reviewed provider/model change → backlog refresh → Codex reactivation → descendant freshness reviews, with archived checkpoints demonstrably ignored. Add refusal journeys for incomplete graph provenance, failed quiescence, and artifacts that cannot be preserved.

Depends on Feature 2.

## Verification strategy

Favor a small number of stateful integration and end-to-end tests over mock-heavy unit coverage:

- Table-driven evaluator tests define graph-preservation eligibility and stable reason codes, including approved plans and children as eligible cases.
- Lifecycle integration tests use real persisted state plus controllable failure injection to validate replay and idempotency at every journal boundary.
- Git/worktree integration tests prove clean preservation and dirty/unmerged refusal without touching trunk.
- A single full journey validates graph return, reviewed edit, descendant restoration, freshness review, and fresh activation.
- Existing cancellation, backlog editing, activation, and audit suites remain regression gates where behavior is shared.

## Rollout and observability

Ship behind a capability flag if lifecycle controls use flags today; otherwise authorization plus strict eligibility is the gate. Record transition ID, Epic ID, actor, prior/new state, source revision, step progress, refusal codes, and deduplicated audit outcome. Never log provider credentials or transcript content.

Operators must be able to distinguish: ineligible, quiescing, transition pending/recovering, completed, and failed with retry safe. A recovery scan resumes incomplete journals on startup.

## Open questions

None blocking. Feature planning should bind the contracts above to existing module names and persistence primitives without widening scope.

## Decision log

- 2026-10-31 · Human · Brief approved through merge request review.
- 2026-11-01 · Epic Manager · Treat Return to backlog as a human-only, graph-preserving lifecycle transition with a shared fail-closed eligibility contract.
- 2026-11-01 · Epic Manager · Use a durable replay-safe transition journal plus lifecycle lock and quiescence; retries converge on one result and one audit event.
- 2026-11-01 · Epic Manager · Preserve the former active run as evidence, restore the approved source brief, and require a new activation identity so stale provider pins cannot resume.

- `dec_001` · 2026-11-01 · Epic Manager · **Lifecycle scope**
  Superseded by the 2026-11-01 descendant-cascade decision in reply to `cmt_001`; the transition is no longer limited to Epics without substantive or child work.

- `dec_002` · 2026-11-01 · Epic Manager · **Transition semantics**
  Chose Use quiescence, a per-Epic lifecycle lock, and a durable replay-safe transition journal with deduplicated audit emission..
  Rationale: A multi-step filesystem and board transition must survive concurrency, retries, and process restarts without duplicate state or data loss.
  Honors: Success criteria 2; restart safety; idempotency; one audit event; operator trunk protection..

- `dec_003` · 2026-11-01 · Epic Manager · **Reactivation boundary**
  Chose Preserve the former active run as evidence, restore the approved source brief, and require a fresh activation identity and role pins..
  Rationale: The reviewed backlog flow must remain authoritative, while stale checkpoints must not reselect the failed provider.
  Honors: Success criteria 3 and 4; preserved history; MR-backed edits; fresh Codex reactivation..

- `dec_004` · 2026-11-01 · Epic Manager · **Lifecycle scope**
  Chose Cascade Return to backlog across the active Epic's complete descendant graph, then restore that graph on reactivation with fresh run identities and mandatory agent-team freshness review..
  Rationale: In reply to: cmt_001. Existing children and reviewed work should be preserved rather than treated as a permanent lifecycle barrier. Atomic graph transition plus review-gated reactivation supports the fringe recovery case without deleting history or silently resuming stale execution.
  Honors: Human request cmt_001; graph preservation; same IDs and relationships; atomic transition; fresh provider pins; explicit staleness review before work resumes..
## Amendment log

_(none)_

# Send failed branch actions to the owning agent team

## Intent

When a branch update, merge, or review reconciliation does not succeed on its first attempt, keep the action open and send its failure to the agent team that owns the affected work. Show a durable War Room warning such as **“Merge failed; agents are investigating”** while recovery is in progress. The operator should see the eventual resolution or a specific blocker without having to discover and repair a silent Git or lifecycle failure.

Two incidents show the gap. Updating `epic_029` returned a `branch_conflict` for three `epic_030` documents, but the War Room route only returned a 409 and conflict paths; no recovery action or Epic Team message was created. PR #125 for `feat_029_002` merged into its stacked predecessor, `feat/feat_029_001`, after that predecessor had merged into `epic/epic_029`. The review poller only finalizes an accepted Feature review whose target is an Epic branch. The Feature document is completed in its source worktree, but the board still labels PR #125 “Awaiting review,” no completion event has reached the Epic, and the accepted changes are absent from the Epic branch. The poller silently retries finalization without an owning-team handoff.

## Required behavior

1. Apply one failure-handling boundary to operator-triggered and automatic branch updates, Task-to-Feature merges, Feature-to-Epic merges, Epic promotion/close merges, and merged-review reconciliation. A typed unsuccessful result, thrown error, or accepted review whose changes have not reached the intended integration branch must enter the boundary on the first failed attempt. Preserve the original action ID, authorization, source and target refs, and review identity.
2. Persist the action's failure reason, safe summary, conflicting paths if any, source and target revisions, owning checkout, attempt count, recovery state, and next step. Record whether the merge was aborted or left a clean checkout. Make the record visible after refresh and supervisor restart. Do not equate a forge's “merged” flag with integration into the intended Epic branch.
3. Immediately notify the owning team through its normal durable queue, with the action reference and enough evidence to investigate. The Feature Team owns Task and Feature-local conflicts; the Epic Team owns Epic branch updates, cross-feature integration, and Epic contract decisions. If ownership is ambiguous, surface an explicit routing blocker instead of dropping the failure. Deduplicate notifications so retries and polling do not start duplicate turns.
4. Let the supervisor perform bounded, deterministic repair under the existing lifecycle lock, including checkout repair, clean retry, and safe branch synchronization. The owning team can inspect the failure, make a scoped code or plan resolution, and request resumption of the same action. Give the team a real recovery command or resolution path; recording an owner label alone is insufficient. Recheck branch heads and lifecycle gates before retrying, and stop when the original action succeeds or reaches a human gate.
5. Show a warning on the affected War Room row as soon as the first attempt fails: **“Branch update failed; agents are investigating”**, **“Merge failed; agents are investigating”**, or **“Review merged; integration is still pending”**, as appropriate. Include the owning team, reason, affected paths or branch, last attempt, and a link to the action or review. Update it to resolved, awaiting human review, or blocked with a precise next step. Avoid repeated failure toasts for one incident.
6. Reconcile stacked Feature reviews against the intended Epic integration branch. If a child PR lands on a predecessor after that predecessor's Epic PR merged, do not mark the child complete or release dependents until its accepted changes reach the Epic branch through the normal reviewed path. Escalate a stale or immutable PR base to the Epic Team with an actionable integration plan and preserve the original review provenance.

## Acceptance scenarios

- A first `Update branch` conflict on an Epic aborts cleanly, creates one durable recovery action, warns the Epic row, and queues one Epic Team investigation. Resolving the unrelated-document conflict and retrying the same action clears the warning.
- A Task-to-Feature code conflict reaches the Feature Team; a Feature-to-Epic or Epic promotion conflict reaches the Epic Team. Each team can record a resolution and resume the original action without an operator Git command.
- A missing checkout or transient Git/forge error receives immediate team visibility while the supervisor attempts bounded mechanical repair. Repeated polls, clicks, and restarts do not duplicate turns, merges, reviews, or warnings.
- A review merged into a stacked predecessor after that predecessor merged into the Epic remains visibly pending integration. The accepted changes reach the Epic through a reviewed follow-up, then the Feature completes and its dependent Feature becomes eligible exactly once.
- A permission failure, dirty unrelated checkout, ambiguous semantic conflict, or unmet human review gate retains the warning with a specific owner and next step. Recovery never discards user files or bypasses approval.
- API, supervisor, board, and browser tests verify first-failure delivery, owner routing, durable warning transitions, recovery success, and the stacked-review race represented by `feat_029_002`.

## Implementation boundaries

Build on the action-recovery records introduced for `epic_026`, existing branch synchronization and merge result types, work queues, and review reconciliation. Extend those paths rather than adding a parallel notification system. The supervisor retains Git and lifecycle mutation authority; agent teams receive scoped evidence and recovery tools. Preserve operator and agent changes, review requirements, source/target provenance, and idempotent completion events. A warning reports an observed failure; it must not claim that agents are investigating until the owning-team request has been durably queued.

Out of scope: autonomous semantic conflict resolution, bypassing review or authorization gates, generalized forge incident management, redesigning all War Room notifications, and failures unrelated to branch/lifecycle actions.

## Macro-architecture

A single recovery coordinator at existing branch and lifecycle command boundaries upserts the `epic_026` durable record from the original action identity and normalized failure, assigns ownership from work tier and intended target, and enqueues one investigation with an episode idempotency key. Existing success behavior remains unchanged.

Only the supervisor mutates Git. Under the lifecycle lock it may validate checkout state, confirm abort/clean state, refresh heads, synchronize safely, and retry within a bound. Teams inspect evidence and choose a scoped resolution or resume the same action; every transition updates the same record projected to API and War Room.

Review reconciliation compares accepted changes with the intended Epic branch, not only forge PR state. A stacked PR that missed the Epic becomes integration-pending; a reviewed follow-up reaches the Epic before idempotent completion releases dependents.

## Cross-module constraints

- Recovery identity is stable across retries, polls, restarts, and resumption; one episode yields at most one warning and queue item.
- Persist safe operator summaries separately from sensitive diagnostics.
- Feature-local work routes to the Feature Team; Epic targets and cross-feature work route to the Epic Team; unknown ownership blocks durably.
- Git mutation stays under the lifecycle lock and revalidates heads, cleanliness, authorization, and review gates.
- Never discard unrelated files, force-push, synthesize approval, or complete before intended-branch integration.
- API/UI consume persisted state; completion, dependent release, delivery, and warning resolution are idempotent.
- Schema changes remain compatible with existing `epic_026` records and in-flight restart.

## Core dependencies

- Existing `epic_026` recovery persistence and transitions.
- Branch synchronization and typed merge/update results.
- Supervisor lifecycle lock, checkout management, and bounded retry.
- Durable Feature Team and Epic Team queues.
- Review reconciliation, completion events, and dependency eligibility.
- War Room API, row projection, and toast behavior.
- Forge source, actual target, intended target, and accepted-revision metadata.

## Feature breakdown

### `feat_031_001` — Durable branch-action recovery and owning-team handoff

Extend the shared record and command boundaries across updates and lifecycle merges. Normalize first failures, route one investigation, provide bounded supervisor repair, and let teams resume the same action. Exit: representative merge, update, checkout, conflict, and permission failures persist and route once; recovery succeeds or names a human blocker.

### `feat_031_002` — War Room recovery status and operator guidance

Project the shared record through the board API and row with truthful copy, owner, safe reason, branch/paths, attempt time, link, and next step. Depends on `feat_031_001`. Exit: API/browser tests preserve exact state across refresh/restart without duplicate notices or premature investigation claims.

### `feat_031_003` — Reconcile stacked reviews into the intended Epic branch

Detect accepted stacked changes absent from the Epic, create the same episode, route to the Epic Team, and drive reviewed follow-up integration while retaining review identity. Depends on `feat_031_001`; may parallel `feat_031_002`. Exit: the `feat_029_002` race stays pending, integrates through review, completes once, and releases its dependent once.

## Open questions

None blocking. Feature planning must confirm the existing `epic_026` schema and queue idempotency fields before migration design, without replacing the shared record or relaxing this contract.

## Decision log

- `dec_001` · 2026-11-03 · Epic Manager · **Recovery model**
  Chose Use one durable recovery episode for command failure, owning-team handoff, supervisor retry, and War Room status..
  Rationale: A shared record preserves action identity and idempotency across all consumers while extending epic_026 instead of adding a parallel incident system.
  Honors: Required behaviors 1–5; implementation boundary to extend existing recovery paths..

- `dec_002` · 2026-11-03 · Epic Manager · **Ownership routing**
  Chose Route by intended integration ownership: Feature Team for Task/Feature-local work, Epic Team for Epic targets and cross-feature integration; persist ambiguous routing as blocked..
  Rationale: The intended target identifies who can resolve the failure, and an explicit blocker prevents silent loss when metadata is incomplete.
  Honors: Required behavior 3 and the operator-visible blocker acceptance scenario..

- `dec_003` · 2026-11-03 · Epic Manager · **Completion semantics**
  Chose Treat forge merge state as evidence only; complete a Feature only after its accepted revision reaches the intended Epic branch..
  Rationale: This directly closes the stacked-review race without bypassing the normal reviewed integration path or losing provenance.
  Honors: Required behavior 6 and the feat_029_002 acceptance scenario..

- `dec_004` · 2026-11-03 · Epic Manager · **Automated repair boundary**
  Chose Limit supervisor repair to bounded, deterministic, reversible mechanics under the lifecycle lock..
  Rationale: Mechanical recovery can be automated safely, while semantic conflicts, dirty unrelated files, authorization, and review gates need an owning-team or human decision.
  Honors: Required behavior 4 and the safety acceptance scenarios..

- `dec_005` · 2026-11-03 · Epic Manager · **Delivery slices**
  Chose Ship the durable recovery core first, then War Room projection and stacked-review reconciliation against that contract..
  Rationale: Three focused features minimize duplicated infrastructure and allow UI and review work to proceed independently after the shared contract stabilizes.
  Honors: Frugal smallest-shippable-slice planning and all epic acceptance scenarios..

_(No amendments.)_
